title: The relationship between the number of repetitions performed at given intensities is different in endurance and strength trained athletes
population: 16 male university students: 8 endurance runners (age 20.9 ± 1.5 years, 63.3 kg; at least 2 years of track or cross-country training at 800 m or more; no resistance training) and 8 weightlifters (22.4 ± 3.3 years, 79.8 kg; at least 2 years of weightlifting, mean 4.1 years).
findings: Each man had a leg press 1RM tested and then, on three further days at least 48 hours apart and in random order, did repetitions to fatigue at 90, 80 and 70% of his 1RM, with a three-second lowering and as fast a lift as possible.
The runners' 1RM was 188.4 ± 13.8 kg and the weightlifters' 335.6 ± 48.6 kg.

Repetitions completed: runners 10.8 ± 3.9 at 90%, 19.8 ± 6.4 at 80% and 39.9 ± 17.6 at 70% of 1RM; weightlifters 7.0 ± 2.1, 11.8 ± 2.7 and 17.9 ± 2.8. The runners did significantly more repetitions than the weightlifters at 70% and 80% (p < 0.05) and not at 90%.

The commonly used repetition tables (those of Baechle and Earle, and of Mayhew and colleagues) predicted the leg press poorly in both groups (the authors' Figure 1 comparison, described in the text). The authors suggest that traditional guidelines may underestimate the repetitions possible at a given percentage, particularly for endurance-trained athletes, and name two explanations: endurance adaptations, or runners' unfamiliarity with heavy loading, which may have made their 1RM test submaximal.
limitations: Eight men a group, one machine exercise, a convenience sample of students, runners with no resistance training whose 1RM may have been under-tested (the authors raise this). The spread among the runners is wide (39.9 ± 17.6 repetitions at 70%). No women, no masters runners, no free-weight squat or hinge, and the runners were young and trained at 800 m or more, not recreational runners of a marathon or ultra. The conflict statement says none.
implications: The only runner data in the corpus on repetitions at a percentage of 1RM: untrained-in-lifting runners did about 11, 20 and 40 leg-press repetitions at 90, 80 and 70% of 1RM, against 7, 12 and 18 for weightlifters. The engine's linear equation with divisor 30 predicts 3, 8 and 13 repetitions at those percentages (computed here, not a finding of the paper). An estimate of a maximum made from repetitions to the limit therefore overstates a runner's maximum, more so as the repetitions rise, which is the direction of less safety margin.

It supports a cap on the repetitions an estimate is made from (`f8.e1rmMaxReps`) and, with the pooled figures of nuzzo-2023-reps-at-percent-1rm, a divisor larger than 30 for lower-body lifts; it does not give a divisor itself.

r1.note: The full text was read on Europe PMC (PMC4042664) on 2026-10-31 with Table 2; every number is from the abstract, Methods or Table 2. The DOI resolves in Crossref, which lists no updated-by notice.

r2.note: Two named authors, both at the School of Sport, Health and Applied Sciences, St Mary's University, Twickenham, as Europe PMC holds. No separate university record was fetched. Conflict statement: none. Cleather is also an author of graham-2021-rir-autoregulation-fixed.

r3.note: Published April 2014, not corrected. nuzzo-2023-reps-at-percent-1rm (2023) cites studies in which endurance athletes did more repetitions at 75% of 1RM or less and says the data are too few to analyse them; it does not supersede this study.

r4.note: Agreed in direction by nuzzo-2023-reps-at-percent-1rm (a meta-regression noting that endurance athletes can do more repetitions at loads up to 75% of 1RM, from three studies it did not analyse) and by the earlier studies this paper cites (Desgorces; Panissa), which were not read. At 90% of 1RM the two groups did not differ here.

r5.note: Population stated: 8 young male middle-distance and cross-country runners without lifting experience, leg press only. Use for recreational and ultra runners, women, older runners and free-weight lifts is extrapolated and labelled so.

r6.note: A journal paper keeps the level of its design (a small cross-sectional study, level C); the caps by class are for sources outside the journals.
